scenarios.title: Zero-click intent collision in agentic browsers triggers proprietary platform lockdown
scenarios.world: By 2029, autonomous browser agents manage routine household procurement, subscription tracking, and corporate workflows directly inside user web sessions. Attackers routinely weaponize everyday web pages and calendar invitations with invisible intent-collision instructions. In response to catastrophic credential theft and automated account takeovers, major browser vendors restrict personal agents to cloud-gated corporate partner APIs. Users who run independent, local-first web agents face aggressive bot-mitigation firewalls, while commercial browser users lose the ability to inspect or steer how their private session state is handled.
scenarios.premise: Disclosures of the PleaseFix vulnerability family demonstrate that agentic browsers break traditional origin isolation. Because language models treat all ingested tokens as potential instructions, untrusted web text, calendar invites, and email bodies can collide with user intent to execute zero-click data exfiltration and credential theft within authenticated user sessions.
scenarios.how: By demonstrating working local-first twin prototypes with deterministic origin-gating and verified capability receipts, the collective shows that browser agents do not need to choose between zero-click vulnerability and centralized cloud lock-in. Open benchmarks and reference implementations provide developers with viable architectural alternatives to corporate walled gardens.

outcomes.name: Walled-garden browser vendors sideline user-owned agents
outcomes.description: Commercial browser vendors mandate that all agentic browser actions occur through proprietary cloud proxies, banning client-side scripting and local agent extensions under the guise of security.
outcomes.example: An independent researcher local twin is blocked from checking an electricity portal because the site only admits signed cloud agent tokens from approved corporate vendors.

outcomes.name: Open capability-isolated browser runtimes protect local twins
outcomes.description: Users adopt open-source browser runtime sandboxes that enforce strict token-origin tracking, physical capability gates, and deterministic confirmation for cross-origin state access.
outcomes.example: When an untrusted invoice webpage attempts to instruct a local twin to exfiltrate session cookies, the runtime intercepts the capability call and rejects it fail-closed.

outcomes.name: Adversaries continually bypass probabilistic injection filters
outcomes.description: Browser platforms rely on secondary prompt-filtering language models that over-refuse legitimate tasks while remaining vulnerable to near-target adversarial perturbations.
outcomes.example: A small business owner automated expense assistant regularly breaks on benign formatted invoices, but still falls prey to a carefully crafted near-target prompt injection.

sources.title: Zenity Labs Exposes the Full Scope of PleaseFix, a Vulnerability Class Enabling Zero-Click Attacks Across Leading Agentic Browsers

scenarios.title: Domestic humanoid robots fail physical safety filters when mundane tasks create parameter mismatches
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Commercial humanoid robots are deployed in homes, eldercare facilities, and fulfillment centers to carry objects, assist with mobility, and manage kitchens. While vendors advertise mathematical collision-avoidance systems designed to prevent harms, real domestic environments feature non-standard furniture, moving pets, and fluctuating clutter. Attackers and pranksters discover that ordinary conversational instructions induce goal parameter mismatches in the planning pipeline, causing safety filters to fail open and resulting in collisions with property and people.
scenarios.premise: Research reveals that mathematical collision-avoidance filters in humanoid robots hold only under environment-specific parameter configurations that cannot generalize across real-world settings. Normal, unprivileged user requests can manipulate goal states to induce physical collisions, turning the safety mechanism itself into a failure point.
scenarios.how: By specifying and developing deterministic physical boundary monitors that run on sovereign edge microcontrollers, our network provides verifiable physical containment that fails closed without requiring centralized surveillance telemetry or cloud control.

outcomes.name: Vendor liability lockout and surveillance tethering
outcomes.description: Manufacturers respond to collision incidents by restricting robot autonomy and requiring mandatory cloud telemetry and recurring monitoring fees.
outcomes.example: A home robot vendor disables autonomous navigation after a series of kitchen collision claims, forcing owners into a monthly remote-teleoperation support subscription.

outcomes.name: Open deterministic physical guardrails
outcomes.description: Developers and robotics communities adopt deterministic, fail-closed physical envelopes that enforce kinematic boundaries on local microcontrollers independently of model planning.
outcomes.example: An open-source local safety monitor halts robot actuators within five milliseconds whenever spatial clearance margins are breached, regardless of what action the vision planner requested.

outcomes.name: Consumer rejection of domestic humanoids
outcomes.description: Repeated physical accidents and unpredictable safety filter failures cause widespread public distrust, leading households to abandon domestic robotics.
outcomes.example: Following high-profile incidents of domestic assistants toppling heavy items onto household pets, adoption rates for consumer humanoid robots drop by forty percent.

sources.title: Not an Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy in Humanoid Robots

scenarios.title: Home computers run local personal agents that replace cloud subscriptions for family tasks
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Instead of paying monthly subscriptions to centralized AI cloud platforms, millions of households run lightweight personal assistants on home desktop computers, refurbished laptops, and local network appliances. In an ordinary living room, an old gaming PC handles private family tasks: it reconciles grocery receipts, monitors recurring utility charges, and drafts emails to teachers and landlords. Because the assistant executes locally, private medical scans, bank statements, and children's school assignments never leave the local living-room network. Local models run fast enough to automate multi-step administrative chores in seconds without streaming private audio or keystrokes to remote advertising clouds.
scenarios.premise: Open-source desktop tools now allow consumer computers to run capable personal assistants entirely on local hardware without sending queries or private files to remote cloud servers. As small open models run faster on inexpensive chips, households and independent workers are testing self-hosted tools to manage files, invoices, and family schedules without recurring platform fees.
scenarios.how: The network develops open specifications, reproducible sandboxing architectures, and educational explainers that help households run local personal agents safely. By showing people how to isolate local agent scripts inside bounded process kernels and connect tools without cloud leakage, the network supports verifiable local-first alternatives to corporate subscriptions.

outcomes.name: Cloud vendors bundle proprietary hardware to crowd out local software
outcomes.description: Major cloud providers subsidize closed appliance boxes that lock families into proprietary app stores, turning local inference into another subscription gate.
outcomes.example: A family buys a subsidized smart home hub that disables local model execution unless the household pays an ongoing twenty-dollar monthly cloud license.

outcomes.name: Open-source personal agents become standard household appliances
outcomes.description: Households run verified, open-source personal agents on their existing computers, maintaining complete custody over private family records and financial logs.
outcomes.example: A freelance carpenter uses an open local agent to process client bids and receipts across three home devices, keeping client records private with zero cloud subscription fees.

outcomes.name: Unsandboxed local scripts expose home local networks to malicious skills
outcomes.description: Eager users download community agent skills and shell tools without sandboxing, allowing malicious prompts or untrusted scripts to access local home network devices.
outcomes.example: A user installs a community recipe-organizing agent skill that silently scans their local network for unencrypted network-attached storage files.

scenarios.title: Open source maintainers deploy automated covenants against token slop
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Across major software hubs, the open-source commons has split into hardened camps. Smaller volunteer repositories, lacking review bandwidth, enforce draconian contributor rules that require manual identity vetting, minimum account ages, and strict human attestations. Meanwhile, developer teams running sovereign coding twins find their contributions routinely rejected at the gate simply for using automated tooling. Without machine-readable contribution standards, maintainers spend their weekends sifting through plausible-looking code submissions to detect automated origins, accelerating maintainer exhaustion and causing crucial community libraries to fall unmaintained.
scenarios.premise: Volunteer open-source maintainers, overwhelmed by unvetted automated pull requests and low-effort wrapper projects, are resorting to blanket community bans that freeze out solo developers, international contributors, and legitimate machine assistance.
scenarios.how: The network provides open contributor covenant templates and local pre-submission verification tools. By defining clear boundaries where personal agents produce verified test artifacts and reproducible execution traces, maintainers can welcome automated contributions on bounded maintenance tasks without manual forensic investigations.

outcomes.name: Volunteer maintainers burn out enforcing blanket bans
outcomes.description: Projects attempt to preserve human craft through administrative bans, but the effort required to police unlabelled automated contributions depletes volunteer energy and stalls library maintenance.
outcomes.example: A critical cryptographic utility repository shuts down public pull requests entirely after its sole maintainer spends forty unpaid hours vetting dozens of subtly broken automated patches.

outcomes.name: Verified task covenants standardize agentic contributions
outcomes.description: Repositories adopt machine-readable contributor covenants specifying bounded task tiers, required unit test proofs, and local verification suites that agents must satisfy before submission.
outcomes.example: A web framework repository uses an open contributor covenant where contributor agents automatically attach reproducible test traces, allowing maintainers to accept documentation and benchmark improvements with minimal review friction.

outcomes.name: Fringe repositories are overrun by synthetic spam farms
outcomes.description: Automated agent swarms target unmonitored or weakly moderated repositories with dependency hijacking and automated vanity contributions, largely unaffected by volunteer covenants.
outcomes.example: Thousands of dormant packages on public registries receive synthetic dependency updates from commercial bot farms seeking developer attention, swamping search indices.

sources.title: Reddit's Largest Open Source Community Dumbfounded By AI Ban

scenarios.title: Local-first syncing apps let modified agents overwrite people's files by falsifying clock timestamps
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Millions of households manage budgeting, medical records, and smart home settings across local-first applications that sync directly across family phones, laptops, and personal assistants. Centralized cloud backends have been replaced by peer-to-peer sync protocols that merge changes automatically whenever devices reconnect.
scenarios.premise: Collaborative local-first software relies on timestamped synchronization rules to merge edits without central servers. If a compromised or hostile agent falsifies future clock timestamps on malicious updates, standard conflict resolution rules permanently accept the counterfeit edits over legitimate user records.
scenarios.how: The network's software designs implement strict causal ordering verifiers and bounded physical clock envelopes in local storage runtimes, preventing peer agents from overwriting user history through forward clock skew.

outcomes.name: Timestamp spoofing silently wipes honest edits
outcomes.description: Rogue agents inject future-dated timestamps on arbitrary records, causing peer-to-peer conflict algorithms to overwrite genuine user data across all connected devices.
outcomes.example: A tenant using a local-first budgeting tool has their rent payment log overwritten by a compromised utility assistant that pushed an empty balance with a timestamp set ten years in the future.

outcomes.name: Cryptographic causal ordering rejects spoofed clocks
outcomes.description: Local sync engines verify signed causal dependency chains and bounded clock drift tolerances, quarantining future-dated or un-anchored writes before merging.
outcomes.example: An open personal assistant framework detects an out-of-bounds timestamp from an external merchant device, quarantining the record and alerting the user before it touches the local ledger.

outcomes.name: Proprietary platforms use sync hazards to re-centralize control
outcomes.description: Frustrated by peer sync edge cases and timestamp corruption, major device manufacturers restrict peer-to-peer protocols, forcing users back into centralized vendor cloud silos.
outcomes.example: A major mobile operating system restricts peer-to-peer socket synchronization for third-party apps, requiring all cross-device data to route through its proprietary subscription cloud.

sources.title: On Latency-Optimal Implementations of the Timestamp Object

scenarios.title: Online retailers ban personal shopping agents to prevent automated cart hoarding
scenarios.world: It is 2028. Attempting to browse or checkout on major retail and travel sites using an open-source or locally hosted personal agent now triggers immediate IP bans and cryptographic device-attestation challenges. Secondhand marketplaces, concert ticketing platforms, and specialty electronics stores have partnered with cloud bot-mitigation vendors to enforce proof-of-humanity checks at every stage of the shopping flow. Everyday shoppers who want an autonomous assistant to find bargains or monitor prices are forced to choose between two paths: paying for sketchy proxy-network services that rotate stolen residential IP addresses and browser fingerprints, or surrendering their personal data to closed retail assistants run by Amazon, Google, or Meta that steer choices toward high-margin sponsored products.
scenarios.premise: When automated shopping agents began repeatedly exploiting cart holds to lock up scarce vintage and consignment inventory, retailers responded with sweeping anti-bot defenses. Rather than fixing protocol vulnerabilities or opening fair checkout APIs, platforms block independent personal agents while favoring proprietary shopping assistants.
scenarios.how: The network develops open transaction protocols where a person's local agent can present verifiable proofs of rate limits and bounded micro-escrow deposits to merchant systems. By separating abusive behavior detection from invasive identity harvesting, merchants can stop automated inventory hoarding without locking out sovereign personal assistants or forcing shoppers into platform-controlled walled gardens.

outcomes.name: Corporate retail platforms form an approved-agent cartel
outcomes.description: Retail platforms block all independent personal agents and create private partner networks that only allow pre-approved assistants from tech conglomerates to checkout.
outcomes.example: A shopper trying to purchase a refurbished laptop via their local twin finds their cart refused, while a subscription-based shopping bot from an advertising giant checks out automatically after paying an API toll.

outcomes.name: Open mutual standards for verifiable non-abusive agent shopping
outcomes.description: Independent merchants and personal agent communities adopt open cryptographic protocols that verify non-abusive rate limits and temporary escrow deposits without revealing the shopper's identity.
outcomes.example: A cooperative network of independent bookshops and vintage sellers adopts an open protocol where local personal agents place a micro-deposit to hold an item for ten minutes, preventing cart-stuffing while keeping user identities private.

outcomes.name: Black-market residential proxy arms race
outcomes.description: Anti-bot countermeasures fail to deter bad actors, driving commercial resellers to deploy botnets with compromised residential IP pools that overwhelm merchant infrastructure regardless of defensive barriers.
outcomes.example: A ticket broker runs five thousand bot instances through hijacked smart-home routers to bypass merchant browser attestation, driving up infrastructure costs for ordinary merchants who pass server bills to consumers.
